paras: The lynching of John Osborne took place on the night of July 2, 1903, when a crowd of several hundred people took Osborne, a young Black man, from two officers on a road near Indian Trail in Union County, North Carolina, and hanged him from a tree. Osborne had been charged with assaulting and robbing Mrs. Lizzie Wentz, an elderly white widow, and had been bound over for trial hours earlier. The Associated Press carried the story nationally, while North Carolina papers presented the hanging as deserved and reported no move to prosecute the mob.

Mrs. Wentz, given as 60 or 64 years old, lived alone about ten miles west of Monroe, and papers dated the alleged assault variously to Saturday night, Sunday night or Monday morning of that week. Osborne, about 24, worked for Joe Biggers near Indian Trail; the Caucasian wrote that suspicion fell on him alone within 48 hours. The Monroe correspondent added that he had been tried and acquitted some years earlier of assaulting a Mrs. Hargett and suspected, without evidence, in an assault near Mint Hill.

Osborne was captured near Indian Trail about three o'clock on the afternoon of July 2. A magistrate, 'Squire Broom (Brown in one report), committed him without bail to await the next term of the Union County Superior Court. The Caucasian placed the hearing at Mrs. Wentz's home, with more than twenty witnesses, and called the evidence "entirely circumstantial": tracks from a hidden mule, a piece of string, and money in his pockets.

After dark Frank Kezziah and Luke Horton, deputized to take him to the Monroe jail, set out by buggy for the Indian Trail station with the prisoner bound with ropes. About two miles along, in dense woods, men stepped from behind trees and dragged Kezziah from the buggy. Kezziah fired a pistol, shots came from the crowd, and both officers were overpowered. The mob then hanged Osborne from the limb of an oak beside the road.

His body was found at dawn less than 500 yards from where the officers were stopped, with no bullet wound, and a South Carolina paper reported that crowds viewed it that afternoon. Wire reports said Osborne was "said" to have confessed.

The New-York Tribune reported that Governor Aycock would send special officers in the hope that some of the mob might be punished. A week later the Caucasian saw no indication of any effort to prosecute the lynchers, and no report of an inquest, arrest or indictment appears in the coverage. The Monroe correspondent called it the county's first lynching in eighteen years and said it was "deplored," while the Charlotte correspondent wrote that no voice had been raised in protest.
White correspondents asserted that Black neighbors had helped gather evidence and called for his death, and that Black men were in the mob.

The Associated Press dispatch from Charlotte ran on July 4 from Maine to Kansas, headed "ASSAULTED WHITE WOMAN" in Portland and "NEGRO TAKEN FROM OFFICERS AND MURDERED" in New Haven. Briefer versions placed Charlotte in South Carolina or named the dead man "Charles Osgood, a negro rape flend," and South Carolina and Maryland weeklies reprinted the story the next week, one as "He Went the Hemp Route."

The Raleigh News and Observer ran three front-page stories in one issue, one headed as a "Ghastly Sequel to the Assault Upon Mrs. Wentz." The Caucasian headlined an "Orderly Body of Citizens" that "Hanged a Self-Confessed Brute," though its text called the evidence circumstantial. In Wilmington, the Semi-Weekly Messenger's editorial on the Evansville riot cited the Union county hanging as proof that Southern "unwritten law" punished only the guilty.

The AP put the mob at several hundred people, the Tribune at two hundred "both whites and blacks," and the Lancaster Ledger at "three hundred white citizens." The Monroe correspondent wrote that a single deputy gave up the prisoner on demand, while other accounts describe two officers and a shot fired; the Times-Dispatch nonetheless headed its account "NOT A SHOT WAS FIRED."

reader.title: Lynching of John Osborne
bases: A Black man accused of assault was taken from two deputized officers by a crowd of several hundred and hanged from a roadside tree (A4, A7, A27).

Osborne, committed by a magistrate to await trial, was seized from officers and hanged by a crowd numbered at two hundred to several hundred (A4, A10, A27); the papers present the hanging as punishment for the assault charge and a Wilmington editorial calls it the 'unwritten law' (A28).

The Associated Press report (A4, A8), separate Charlotte and Monroe specials (A2, A3, A5), the Tribune's own telegraph (A10), a different Charlotte version (A25) and the Caucasian's long account (A27) agree on the seizure from officers and the hanging near Indian Trail.

accounts.label: Associated Press (Charlotte)
accounts.gist: Osborne, given a preliminary hearing and committed, was taken by several hundred people from the two officers conveying him to jail and hanged near Indian Trail; he was 'said' to have confessed, and Kezziah fired one shot before being disarmed.

accounts.label: Charlotte special correspondent
accounts.gist: Men stepped from behind trees in dense woods, dragged Kezziah from the buggy, and shots were fired from a crowd of several hundred; Black neighbors were said to approve the lynching.

accounts.label: Monroe special correspondent
accounts.gist: A single deputy, accosted two miles out by 'a body of men', complied at once with their demand; the body was found at dawn hanging from an oak, and the county's first lynching in eighteen years was 'deplored'.

accounts.label: New-York Tribune telegraph
accounts.gist: A mob of two hundred 'both whites and blacks' took Osborne from two deputy sheriffs early in the morning; the governor would send officers to seek the lynchers.

accounts.label: Lancaster Ledger's Charlotte dispatch
accounts.gist: A mob of 'three hundred white citizens' lynched Osborne early in the morning, and crowds viewed the body that afternoon.

accounts.label: The Caucasian
accounts.gist: Lays out circumstantial evidence from a 20-witness hearing at Mrs. Wentz's home and describes the hanging from an oak by a crowd of several hundred 'including a number of negroes'.

framing.detail: The North Carolina papers headlined him a 'Self-Confessed Brute' hanged by an 'Orderly Body of Citizens' and wrote of 'swift vengeance' visited on 'the negro brute'.
The Wilmington Semi-Weekly Messenger's editorial called it the Southern 'unwritten law' and offered the Union county hanging as proof that only the guilty suffered.
Most out-of-state papers carried the AP story or a brief, some with headlines like 'ASSAULTED WHITE WOMAN' or 'He Went the Hemp Route.'
The New Haven Journal and Courier ran the AP text under 'NEGRO TAKEN FROM OFFICERS AND MURDERED' while retaining its 'full confession' claim.
The Monroe correspondent called it the county's first lynching in eighteen years and said it was 'deplored', while still describing it as Osborne 'paying the penalty of his crime'.
